files.name: 01-getting-started.md
files.text:
# Getting started

Prospektor Studio is a workspace where a sales team researches target
companies and drafts partner pitches. You type a company; the studio works
out who that company actually is from its own website, researches it, scores
partnership fit against what your workspace says it is hunting for, and
drafts your enabled deliverables — pitch deck, one-pager, cold-email
sequence, written proposal — plus a decision-maker list and lookalike
companies to pitch next.

## Your first minutes

- **Sign-in** is Google SSO or an emailed magic link — there are no
  passwords. Access is your workspace's email allowlist; if your address is
  on it, you are in.
- A brand-new workspace opens with a short **interview** (three questions —
  what to hunt for, a deal that already worked, how you want to sound) asked
  while the studio researches your company in the background. Every answer
  sharpens future pitches; you can skip and come back via
  [Workspace settings](/settings).
- The **guided tour** walks the screens once on your first landing;
  you can bring it back by unticking "Do not show this again" on its last
  step next time it shows, and skipping it never loses anything.
- The home screen, [Suggested](/), proposes companies worth pitching next,
  one card at a time — a thumbs-up starts a real pitch immediately.
- Stuck at any point? **Support**, at the foot of the sidebar, opens a chat
  that answers in seconds and remembers where you left off; its
  **💡 Request a feature** toggle sends an idea, an improvement or a bug
  report straight to the Prospektor team.

## The core loop

1. Open [New pitch](/pitch/new), enter a company name or domain (the field
   autocompletes and warns if your team already pitched them).
2. The run takes minutes and shows six live stages — understand, research,
   score, draft, people, check. You can leave any time: runs continue in the
   background and are listed under [Running](/running).
3. The finished pitch lands in the [Library](/library): summary, fit thesis,
   signals for and against, deliverables, decision-makers, lookalikes.
4. Edit any deliverable in place (the pencil). Saved edits teach the studio
   your team's voice — tone only, never facts — so future pitches sound more
   like you.
5. Record what happened in [Outcomes](/outcomes) — closed deals feed the
   Suggested shelf, so what it offers drifts toward what actually closes.

## This documentation

Everything the Support chat knows lives in these pages, and they are also
published at [prospektor.ai/help](https://prospektor.ai/help) — searchable,
and always describing the version of the studio that is actually running.

files.name: 02-screens.md
files.text:
# The screens, and where each one lives

Every screen has a real URL. When pointing someone somewhere, use these
exact paths.

| Screen | Path | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Suggested (home) | `/` | Companies the studio proposes pitching next, one card at a time, plus tiles for Call prep and Inbound prospecting |
| New pitch | `/pitch/new` | The form: company name or domain, optional contact, motion and value angle from your workspace's own vocabulary; ⚡ Beast Mode at its foot for a whole list |
| Running | `/running` | Runs in flight; Watch drops into the live terminal; a stuck run can be dismissed, a live one stopped |
| Library | `/library` | Saved pitches, sortable, with unread markers; each card offers Call prep and "What happened?" |
| A pitch | `/pitches/<id>` | One run — live while it works, the finished pitch after |
| Outcomes | `/outcomes` | What each prospect turned into: a stage ladder plus free-text notes; "Make sense of this" reads a record back |
| Call prep | `/prep` | One sheet for a specific upcoming call — goal, framing, talking points, the likely objection with an answer |
| Evaluate inbound | `/evaluate` | Paste outreach somebody sent you, get an honest take-the-call-or-skip-it with reasons |
| Your network | `/network` | Import who the team knows (LinkedIn export or pasted list) — the raw material for warm paths |
| Shared links | `/shares` | Every pitch shared outside the workspace, who opened it and when; Revoke kills a link immediately |
| Workspace settings | `/settings` | The brief — facts, voice, guardrails, banned terms — plus who has access, the deliverable stylesheet, Appearance (light / dark / system) and the danger zone |
| Portfolio uploads | `/portfolio` | Agencies only: how your last portfolio upload is going, and the ones before it |

Every screen is a row on the left sidebar, in three groups: **Work**
(Suggested, New pitch, Running, Library, Outcomes), **Prepare** (Call prep,
Evaluate inbound) and **Workspace** (Your network, Shared links, Settings).
The workspace switcher sits at the sidebar's head — click your workspace
name to switch workspaces, set **Appearance** (light / dark / system),
create a client workspace or upload a whole
portfolio of them (agencies), or sign out. An agency workspace is tagged
**(Agency)** in that list with its client workspaces indented under it.
Support sits at the sidebar's foot, next to who you are signed in as.
On a narrow window the sidebar collapses to its icons.

files.name: 03-pitches.md
files.text:
# Pitches — runs, results, editing

## Starting a run

[New pitch](/pitch/new) takes a company name, a bare domain, or both, plus
optionally a point of contact, the partnership motion to argue for, and the
value angle to lead with (the last two come from your workspace's own brief).
Before anything else, the studio works out **who the company actually is**
from its own website — it opens the site, reads what they sell and to whom,
and rules out same-named businesses. The pitch is then researched, scored
and drafted against that settled identity.

## While it runs

A run takes minutes and shows six named stages: understand, research, score,
draft, people, check — with what each stage is actually doing ("2 searches ·
9 sources read"). There is no percentage bar on purpose: research is one
stage of six, and a long read would sit at 17% looking dead.

**You can leave.** The worker runs in the background; [Running](/running)
lists every run in flight with Watch to drop back in. A run nothing has been
heard from in twenty minutes is marked stopped and offers **Dismiss**; a run
still working offers **Stop** (confirmed — it kills real work). There is no
pause.

**Everybody reads every run; your own are yours to manage.** Stopping,
archiving or deleting a run somebody else started — or calling off their
batch — needs the owner or admin role in the workspace. Reading it never
does. (The roles are in [Workspace settings](/help/08-workspace).)

## Beast Mode — a whole list at once

The foot of the New pitch form: upload a CSV or paste one company per line
(`Company name, website` — the website optional) and **Run batch →** queues
every row through the same pipeline. Up to 100 companies per batch, three
running at once, each landing in the Library like any other pitch. The CSV
is parsed in your browser and never uploaded.

## Reading the result

A pitch reads as a sequence: Summary → Fit thesis → Signals (for and
against, each rated by recency and recurrence) → Deliverables (deck,
one-pager, cold email, proposal — each block copyable and pencil-editable) →
Decision-makers → Lookalikes → Next steps. If it is coral, you can click it.

- **Blank decision-maker names are deliberate.** A name appears only when a
  credible source supports it; blanks are left for your own enrichment
  rather than filled with guesses.
- **Bracketed placeholders** in drafts mark what could not be verified —
  filling them in is your job, and they are listed together so none is
  missed.
- **Find more** under the researched lists queues more research in the
  background — an empty box is a valid instruction ("look again").
- **Compliance findings**: the studio reads its own draft back and reports
  anything that broke a rule (banned terms, numbers without provenance)
  next to the work. What to do about them is your call.

## Editing, and what it teaches

The pencil on any deliverable block edits it in place. **Saved edits become
brand-voice examples for future runs** — tone and structure only, never
facts, and facts never cross companies. Editing is the highest-leverage
thing a team does in the studio.

Since 23 Aug 2026 a run chooses those examples **for the company it is
working on** rather than simply taking the three most recent: the ones whose
subject looks most like this target, with at least one example of each
deliverable the run has to write. So a workspace with fifty saved edits
draws on all fifty, a few at a time, instead of on whichever three were
saved last.

A run also carries what your team recorded in [Outcomes](/outcomes) — what
actually won and lost, in their words. The waiting line says so while the
run works: *"Brief loaded, with 4 of your edits as voice references and what
you recorded about 6 companies."* It shapes the judgment, never the copy — a
company from your own outcomes record appearing in a deliverable is flagged by
the compliance check like a banned word is.

## Ask the studio

The last tab of a finished pitch is a conversation about it — where a claim
came from, how to open the first call, what to say when the predicted
objection lands. It answers only from that pitch and your brief, and never
changes the pitch. Each member has their own conversation per pitch; it
survives reloads.

## Print / PDF

Ctrl/Cmd-P, or the Print / PDF button on a pitch or a share, prints the
deliverable styled with your workspace's own stylesheet — Save as PDF in the
same dialog is the PDF export.

files.name: 04-sharing.md
files.text:
# Sharing a pitch

**Share this pitch** on a finished pitch's Summary sends the whole thing;
**Share** on a single deliverable's tab sends just that document. Either
mints a short `/p/<token>` link.

- A full share carries the whole run — fit score, signals, decision-makers,
  lookalikes, every deliverable — styled with your workspace's stylesheet.
  That is your prospecting on a named company: forwarding the link outside
  your team hands it over.
- Narrowing a share to one deliverable sends the document and **none of the
  research**.
- The recipient meets a **gate first**: who sent it, what company it is
  about, and a sign-up. The content is not in the page until an account
  exists. Any signed-in account can read it — but **a share grants sight of
  one pitch, never entry to your workspace**.
- [Shared links](/shares) lists every link the team has sent, who opened it
  and when. **Revoke** is one click and works immediately, including for
  someone who already read it. **A link is yours to revoke if you minted it**;
  pulling a colleague's link needs the owner or admin role, because it goes
  dead in the recipient's hands and nothing tells the person who sent it.
  (See [Workspace settings](/help/08-workspace) for what the roles are.)
- **If the workspace is paused, every link it has sent pauses with it.**
  Anyone opening one is told it is temporarily unavailable — not that it was
  taken back, and nothing about why. No work, no research and no stylesheet
  is served while the workspace is locked, and every link that was not
  revoked comes back the moment the workspace does. Revoking still works
  from the locked screen's side of the wall — a paused link is not a dead
  one, and killing it for good is the one thing a locked workspace still
  lets you do.
- **A share link is not findable in search.** The gate already kept the work
  itself out of the page until an account exists, and the studio now tells
  search engines to keep the whole of `studio.prospektor.ai` — the gate
  included — out of their index. A link is private because you only sent it to
  the people you sent it to; nothing puts it in front of anyone else.
- Speaker notes, compliance findings and the research log never travel on a
  share.

files.name: 05-network.md
files.text:
# Your network, and warm paths

A pitch ends with decision-makers to approach cold; the warmer question is
who your team already knows who could open the door.

## Importing your network

[Your network](/network) (sidebar, under Workspace) takes the knowledge as
data, without
any integration. The screen is one main act — paste a list — with the two
file imports behind the ghost buttons below it, and the small ⓘ by the
title holding the fine print:

- **A pasted list**: pick a category — Investors, Partners, Customers,
  Advisors, Friends & former colleagues, or *Other…* to name your own —
  then one per line, who then how-you-know-them after a dash. A minute of
  typing, no file needed. Press **Add the list**.
- **A LinkedIn export, per member** (*Import LinkedIn connections*): from
  LinkedIn, Settings & Privacy → Data privacy → "Get a copy of your data" →
  tick Connections → Request archive; LinkedIn emails the `Connections.csv`
  within ~10 minutes, and it uploads here. Re-uploading replaces your
  previous import rather than double-counting. **Email addresses in the
  export are dropped at import and never stored** — the studio keeps who and
  where, never how to email a stranger.
- **An email address book, per member** (*Import your email address book*),
  with instructions per provider:
  - **Google (Gmail / Google Workspace)**: contacts.google.com → Export (in
    the left sidebar) → Google CSV, then upload the file here.
  - **Outlook / Office 365**: outlook.office.com/people → Manage contacts →
    Export contacts → all contacts → Export, then upload the file here.

  What is kept per contact: name, company, job title. **Email addresses,
  phone numbers and everything else in the file are dropped at import and
  never stored.** Re-uploading replaces your previous address book import.
- **A written `## Network` section** in the brief, for ties that read
  better as prose.

Every import is attributed to the member who brought it, and only that
member can remove it. Importing calls no model, and nothing network-shaped
ever travels on a shared link.

## Warm paths

With a network in the workspace, every finished pitch gains a **Warm paths**
panel: ranked *you → connector → target* paths, each connector actually in
your network, each claim evidenced with the page it was read on (or the line
of your own data that states it). The best path comes with a **forwardable
intro request** drafted in your voice. An honest "checked these, found
nothing" is a normal result.

It runs by itself as a follow-on of each pitch run when the workspace has a
network, and on demand from the panel (**Find warm paths** / **Look
again**) — useful for pitches that predate an import.

## Connection-degree chips

Every decision-maker row carries **1st · 2nd · 3rd+** chips — LinkedIn
people-search links pre-filtered by degree. They open in your own logged-in
LinkedIn, so the degrees are yours; a teammate clicking the same chips sees
their own network. The studio never reads LinkedIn — it only writes search
URLs.

files.name: 06-calls.md
files.text:
# Call prep, and evaluating inbound

## Call prep — "we have a call with these guys"

[Call prep](/prep) (tiles on the home screen, on every library card, and on
a finished pitch) asks the one thing the studio cannot infer — **which call
it is**: first call, discovery, pitch, negotiation, or kickoff — plus an
optional sentence about the call, and hands back one sheet: the goal for
exactly that call, how to frame it, three to five grounded talking points,
the questions to ask, the objection they will actually raise with an answer
sayable verbatim, and the ask to end on.

Name a company with a saved pitch and the pitch's research rides along whole
— the sheet lands in under a minute and says what it drew on. A prep is a
call sheet, not a pitch: it never appears in the Library, and it is copyable
as plain text. The recent list on the prep screen keeps a morning's sheet
findable before the 3pm call.

## Evaluate inbound — "is this call worth taking?"

[Evaluate inbound](/evaluate) (the Inbound prospecting tile) is prep's
mirror: paste the outreach somebody sent — the cold email, the LinkedIn
message, the "quick 15-minute chat?" — and the studio reads it against what
your workspace is hunting for and answers plainly: **take the call or skip
it**, with who the sender turns out to be, what they are actually asking for
once the framing is stripped, the argument from your own brief, red flags,
and — when the verdict is a lean — the questions worth sending back first.

A **take** verdict hands straight into Call prep with the sender prefilled.
Evaluations are listed as recent verdicts on their screen — never in the
Library, because a judgment is not a pitch.

files.name: 07-outcomes.md
files.text:
# Outcomes — what actually happened

[Outcomes](/outcomes) is where your team records what each pitch turned
into, per prospect company: a stage off a short ladder — found the right
contact, had a meeting, closed the deal — or how it ended (went quiet, not a
fit, lost), plus free-text notes taken verbatim: call notes, a pasted email
thread, "they bought because the CFO wanted the one-pager". Low friction is
the design — structure is the studio's job, not yours.

- The record is per **company**, not per pitch: an inbound deal that closed
  without a run still gets a record, and two runs on one target are one
  relationship.
- The door is **What happened?** on every library card and on a finished
  pitch; library cards wear the stage as a badge.
- **Make sense of this** has the studio read the whole record back and
  propose, beside the notes, what actually won or lost this one — anchored
  in the notes' own words — and the few follow-up questions worth answering
  next. It never changes the record; **Look again** is the update story.
- Companies recorded as **closed** feed the Suggested shelf's next refill as
  its strongest evidence, so what the shelf offers drifts toward what
  actually closes.
- **And since 23 Aug 2026, what you record shapes what the studio writes.**
  A bounded digest of your own record — where each prospect got to, how it
  ended, the studio's reading of it where you asked for one, and your team's
  newest notes in their own words — now rides every pitch run, every call
  prep and every inbound evaluation. Wins and losses both: a deal that died
  on implementation time teaches the next draft as much as one that closed.
  The records closest to the company being worked on go first, and the
  record for that exact company always travels when you have one.
- It stays inside the studio. The studio is told, in the prompt itself, that
  nothing from your outcomes goes into a deliverable — not a quote, not a
  number, not the name of another company you have been talking to — and that
  nothing there is to be looked up on the web. And because an instruction is
  not a guarantee, the same check that reads every draft back for banned words
  now also flags any company from your own outcomes record that turns up in
  the copy, next to the block it turned up in. Your pipeline steers the
  writing; it is not material to send.
- So the studio does get better the more you use it, and outcomes are the
  loop that makes that true. A workspace that has recorded fifty deals runs
  differently from one opened this morning.

files.name: 08-workspace.md
files.text:
# Workspace settings, members, billing

## The brief

[Workspace settings](/settings) holds the brief — the facts, voice,
guardrails and banned terms every pitch is drafted against, plus what the
studio has learned from your team's edits. The studio writes to the brief
while it is still researching a new workspace; **saving the brief yourself
takes it over for good** — the studio stops writing to it, and later
research is dropped rather than merged over a human's corrections.

**The `allowedEmails` block is the one part of the brief the editor does not
own.** Who can sign in is changed on the access list further down the same
page, never by typing in the brief: an edit that changes those lines saves
everything else and leaves the list where it was. That is deliberate — the
brief is a text box every member of the workspace can reach, and who belongs
here should not be one edit away from anybody who can type.

## Appearance — light, dark, or your machine's

**Where it is:** click your workspace's name at the top of the sidebar — the
same menu that holds your other workspaces and Sign out — and **Appearance**
is at its foot. It is also on [Workspace settings](/settings), near the
bottom. Both are the same control; changing one moves the other.

The menu is the quicker one, and it stays open while you click, so you can
try light against dark with the studio visible behind it.

Three settings:

- **System** — follow whatever this computer is set to, and keep following
  it. A machine that switches to dark at sunset switches the studio with
  it, with no reload. This is the setting you start on.
- **Light** — always light, whatever the machine says.
- **Dark** — always dark.

Two things worth knowing:

**It is saved on the device you set it on, not on the workspace.** Your
colleagues are not affected, and neither are your other workspaces —
switching between clients never changes the studio's colour. Set it again
on your laptop and your desktop if you want it in both places. A browser
in private mode forgets it when the window closes.

**Deliverables stay on white paper in either theme.** A deck, one-pager,
proposal or email is what your client will be looking at, so it is rendered
the same way in both — a white sheet inside the dark studio. Shared links
are all deliverable, so a share page is always light, whatever the person
reading it has their machine set to. Printing is light for the same reason.

## Members and access

Access is the workspace's email allowlist, managed from Workspace settings by
its **owner** or an **admin** — named addresses only. Removing an address takes
effect immediately. Sign-in is Google SSO or an emailed magic link; there are no
passwords to reset.

### Who added whom, and when

Every entry on the access list carries a line saying who put it there and on
what date. It is there because "there is an address on this list and I cannot
tell whether I added it" is a question the product should never make you guess
at.

Three things worth knowing about that line:

- **It starts from when we built it.** Anything that was already on your list
  says *added before Prospektor recorded this*, and nothing can fill it in
  after the fact. Inventing a plausible name would be worse than the gap.
- **A whole-company entry** — one that looks like `@yourcompany.com` — shows
  the door it came through and no person, because nobody chose it: buying with
  a company address puts that company's domain on the list, which is how your
  colleagues walk in without being invited one at a time. Once an owner has
  settled it (below) the line also says *kept by* them, and the date.
- **Some entries name a door instead of a person**: *by Prospektor* when we put
  an address on by hand, or *by their agency* when the agency that set the
  workspace up did. We do not show you an address belonging to somebody who is
  not on your own list.

### Everyone at your company can sign in — keep it, or narrow it

If you bought with a company address, your access list carries an entry like
`@yourcompany.com` as well as your own address, and the list now says in words
what it means: **everyone at that company can sign in, including addresses that
do not exist yet.** That is how it has always worked; what is new is that the
product says so, and that you get to decide about it.

Two answers, and only an owner may give either:

- **Keep** — you are happy for the whole company to walk in. Nothing changes
  except that the list stops asking, and records that you decided it.
- **Narrow** — the grant comes off, and from then on only the named addresses
  on your list can sign in. Everyone else at your company is signed out
  immediately.

**Narrowing cannot be undone from inside Prospektor.** Nothing in the product
grants a whole company again — not settings, not us. If you narrow and then
want a colleague back, add their address by name. Keeping, on the other hand,
is not a lock: you can narrow a grant you kept, later, whenever you like.

### Somebody from another company needs the owner's yes

Adding a colleague — anybody at a company already on your access list — works
the way it always has: type the address, press Add, done.

Adding somebody from a **different** company is different if you are an admin
rather than the owner. It becomes a **request**: the address is not added, that
person cannot sign in, and the owner sees it on their own access list with
*Approve* and *Decline* beside it. You will see it on yours too, marked as
waiting for them.

This exists because letting a fourth party read every pitch a workspace has run
is the owner's call — most often it is the agency that administers a workspace
asking the client who owns it. An owner adding somebody from another company
just adds them; there is nobody for them to ask.

Approving lets that person in exactly as an ordinary add does, and the access
list then shows both names: who asked, and who approved. Declining leaves
nothing behind — the person was never able to sign in, and is never told they
were asked about.

### You are told when access changes

If you own or administer a workspace, you get an email whenever an address is
added to it, removed from it, or given a role — saying what changed, who did it,
and linking straight to the access list. A role change also emails the person
whose role moved, which matters most when it moved down: losing a role is
otherwise invisible until you try to use it.

You also get one when an admin **asks** to add somebody from another company —
headed *approval needed*, because nobody has been let in — and the admin who
asked is emailed if you decline. Keeping a whole-company grant emails nobody:
nothing about who can sign in changed.

You are not emailed about your own clicks, and somebody you have just added
gets the invite instead of this notice. If nobody is recorded as the workspace's
owner — which is true of a few of the oldest workspaces — the notice has nobody
to go to and none is sent; ask us and we will set an owner.

### Telling somebody they have access

Adding an address lets somebody in; it does not tell them. Every named entry
on the access list carries an **invite** link beside it — click it and that
person gets the same email an agency's client contact gets: what the
workspace is, who set it up, and a sign-in link with their address already
filled in. Use it for anyone who was added quietly, for a workspace made
before invites existed, and for a client who says the first one never
arrived — sending it twice is fine. Whole-domain entries (`@example.com`)
have no single inbox behind them, so they carry no invite link.

## Roles: owner, admin, member

Every named address on the access list holds one of three roles, shown beside it
on the list. **Your role** on that same page says which one is yours and lists
what it lets you do — and what it does not, with the role that would.

**The short version: the ladder is about who joins, who administers and who
destroys. It is not a read/write split.** A member runs pitches and call preps,
reads every run in the workspace, edits any deliverable, edits the brief's
prose, mints share links and imports their own network. None of that changes
with your role.

- **Member** — everything in the paragraph above. This is what everybody is
  unless somebody says otherwise.
- **Admin** — a member, plus the workspace's configuration: adding and removing
  people on the access list, sending invites, uploading the deliverable
  stylesheet, accepting or dismissing a rescan of the brief, managing a run or
  a share link somebody else started, and (in an agency workspace) creating
  client workspaces.
- **Owner** — an admin, plus the things nobody else may do: **delete the
  workspace**, **change roles**, **settle a whole-company grant** (keep it, or
  take it off the list for good), and **approve or decline somebody from
  another company** that an admin has asked to add.

The account that created a workspace is its owner — with one deliberate
exception, which is the whole of the next section: **when an agency creates a
workspace for a client and names the client's email address, that client is the
owner and the agency is an admin.**

### Changing somebody's role

Only an owner can. On the access list, each named address has a small role
picker under it; choosing a role applies it at once, and everybody who owns or
administers the workspace is emailed about it — including the person whose role
changed.

**Handing the workspace over** is the same picker: choose **owner** for
somebody else and you step down to admin in the same act. You keep members and
the stylesheet; you lose deletion and roles. It is one action rather than two,
so the workspace is never briefly owned by two people or by none.

**A workspace can never be left with no owner.** Demoting the last one,
removing them from the access list, or asking us to free their address is
refused with a message saying so — because appointing an owner is itself an
owner's job, so there would be no way back. Give somebody else the owner role
first.

### What an admin cannot do to an owner

An admin adds and removes **members**. They cannot remove an owner, and they
cannot remove another admin — only somebody above a person can take their access
away. Removing yourself always works, whatever your role.

## If an agency set your workspace up

Some workspaces are created by an agency or consultancy that runs Prospektor
for their clients. If yours is one of them, [Workspace settings](/settings)
carries a section called **The agency above this workspace**: who they are,
which addresses on your own access list are theirs, and how either side ends
the arrangement.

### The workspace is yours

**When the agency named your email address as they created the workspace, you
own it and they are an admin of it.** In practice that means they keep doing
everything they do for you — running pitches, adding your colleagues, uploading
your deliverable stylesheet, settling a rescan of your brief — and there are
exactly two things they cannot do:

- **They cannot delete your workspace.** Deletion is the owner's, and the owner
  is you.
- **They cannot remove you from it.** An admin removes members, never an owner.

You can also do everything an owner does anywhere else: change roles, approve
somebody from another company, settle a whole-company grant, and hand the
workspace to a colleague.

Two honest limits:

- **A workspace created without your email address on the form belongs to the
  agency**, because at the moment it was made there was nobody else to give it
  to. That includes every row of a portfolio upload. The agency hands it over
  when you are on the list — see below.
- **Workspaces created before 23 August 2026 were not changed.** Nobody's
  ownership moved because we shipped a release. If your agency owns your
  workspace and you would rather own it, ask them to hand it over — or ask us.

### Hand over to the client

An agency that owns a client's workspace hands it over from the same settings
section: **Hand over to the client**, which makes the named client address the
owner and steps the agency down to admin **in one action**. Nothing is briefly
owned by two people or by none, and nothing about the work changes.

If the client's own address is not on the access list yet, the section says so
instead of offering a button that cannot work — add them, then hand over.

### Detaching — either side, immediately

Either side can end the arrangement, at any time, without the other side's
agreement and with no waiting period:

- **The client's owner** presses *Detach from ⟨agency⟩*, and the agency's
  addresses come off the access list.
- **The agency** presses *Detach from this client* from inside that workspace,
  and does the same to its own addresses.

**Nothing is deleted, on either side.** Every pitch, call prep, share link,
saved edit, network import and outcome stays exactly where it is, in the
workspace, with whoever keeps it. Detaching removes access and the connection
between the two workspaces; it removes no work.

Three things worth knowing:

- **It takes effect at once, and both sides are emailed.** There is no window in
  which the other side can stop it. If somebody can veto your leaving, you have
  not really been able to leave — so nobody can.
- **The agency cannot detach from a workspace it is the only way into.** That
  would leave a workspace nobody can open. The message says the way out: hand
  it over to the client first, then detach.
- **A client whose agency was paying will be asked to pay.** If the agency's
  subscription stops covering the workspace it will pause, and the lock screen's
  *Re-subscribe* button reopens the same studio — everything kept — against your
  own card. Nothing is deleted while it is paused. A **paused** workspace cannot
  be detached from until it is reopened, because a paused workspace answers
  nothing: re-subscribe first, then detach.

If a detach happened in error, the two halves go back separately: the
workspace's owner adds the addresses again from the access list, and we can
re-seat the connection between the two workspaces. Ask support.

## More than one workspace

An account can belong to several workspaces; the switcher at the sidebar's
head — your workspace's name — lists them all and switches between them.

An agency workspace — one that can create workspaces for its clients — is
marked **(Agency)** in that list, and the client workspaces it created are
indented beneath it. With ten workspaces on one account, the one that runs
the others is the one you can find at a glance.

Agency-flagged workspaces additionally get **New client workspace** in that
menu, for the agency's **owner or admins** — name the client and a live,
researched workspace exists before the next screen. A plain member of an agency
workspace cannot create client workspaces: each one is a workspace that will be
billed, with your agency's name on somebody else's screen.

**Who owns what that form creates.** Name the client contact's email and **the
workspace is theirs** — that address is its owner and you are its admin, so you
run it for them but cannot delete it or remove them. Leave the contact field
empty and the workspace stays yours until you hand it over (*Hand over to the
client*, on its settings screen). Either way you can end the arrangement later,
and so can they: see [If an agency set your workspace
up](#if-an-agency-set-your-workspace-up) above, which is written for the client
and is worth reading before you explain it to one.

Name the client contact's email and they also get an **invite email** — it says
your agency set the workspace up for them, names you, says in plain words that
the workspace is theirs and what you can and cannot do with it, and links
straight to sign-in with their address prefilled. The tick-box is on by
default; untick it to set things up quietly and invite them later. Whether the
invite was sent (or could not be) is shown the moment you land in the new
workspace. That invite belongs to this one-at-a-time form; a portfolio upload
mails nobody.

## A whole portfolio at once

Below that form, **Portfolio upload** points the same act at a list. Paste
one company per line — `Company name, website`, the website optional — or
choose a CSV and it is read into the box. Extra columns are ignored, and a
header row is recognised as the format rather than treated as a company.
Every row becomes its own client workspace with the research already reading
that company's site. **A portfolio row names no contact, so each of those
workspaces is owned by your agency** until you hand it over — there is nobody
else to give it to at the moment it is made.

- **The agency's owner or an admin presses it**, the same rule as the
  one-at-a-time form beside it. Anyone in the workspace can open the results
  screen and watch.
- **Up to 50 companies per upload**, three researched at a time. A longer
  list is refused with the number in the message rather than quietly cut
  short; split it and upload the rest as a second portfolio.
- **Rows that cannot be used are named, one by one** — a line that is
  neither a company name nor a website, the same company twice, or a
  company your agency already has a workspace for.
- **You stay where you are.** Creating one workspace moves you into it;
  creating forty cannot, so the switcher gains them and you stay in the
  agency. A results screen shows every row filling in, and it has an
  address: [`/portfolio`](/portfolio) reopens your newest upload and lists
  the ones before it. Leave it and come back — the upload keeps going with
  the tab closed.
- **Nobody is emailed.** Each new workspace starts nearly empty on the
  completeness bar in its own [Workspace settings](/settings), and that
  bar is the list of what its company still needs to answer. Send them
  their workspace link when you are ready for them.

Creating client workspaces — one at a time or a portfolio at a time — is
**free during the beta**. Per-workspace billing arrives later: at creation
you will choose whether it bills your agency or your client pays to unlock
their workspace.

## The deliverable stylesheet

Workspace settings → Deliverable stylesheet (owner or admin): upload a CSS file
and every deliverable — on screen, on shares, in print — is styled with it.
The studio's own chrome never changes; the stylesheet reaches your work and
nothing else.

## What Prospektor can see about your workspace

Prospektor keeps an operator view of every workspace **as a record**, so
accounts can be set up, paused and supported without anybody at Prospektor
being added to your allowlist. It holds the workspace's name and id, who it
was provisioned for, its plan, whether it is paused, the addresses on its
access list — and, since 23 Aug 2026, **how much it is used**: when somebody
was last signed in, how many sign-ins there have been, how many pitch runs,
call preps and other research the workspace has run, and what those cost
Prospektor to run.

Those are **counts and dates only**. Nothing records your navigation — no page
views, no searches, no dwell time, no analytics and no session recording of any
kind. And the operator view does not open your work: pitches, your brief's
prose, share links and your voice examples still need to be on this workspace's
own access list, which nobody at Prospektor is unless you put them there.

Two things are deliberately outside that rule and are named here because they
are. **Feature requests** you send through the composer, and **support chat
conversations**, are both read by the Prospektor team — the first is a message
to them by definition, the second so that a question that keeps coming up
becomes a fix. Each of those records the studio screen you were on when you
wrote it, because "where were they when this went wrong" is most of what makes
a bug report useful. That is the only place a screen is ever recorded, and only
for something you deliberately sent.

## Billing, pausing, deleting

- The subscription is **$999/month per workspace**, taken by Stripe through
  prospektor.ai — the studio itself holds no card details.
- A **paused** workspace means the subscription behind it lapsed; the lock
  screen's resubscribe button reopens the same studio with everything kept.
- **Workspace deletion** lives in Workspace settings' danger zone, and only an
  **owner** may use it — not an admin, deliberately: it is the one act in the
  product that cannot be undone. Deletion removes the workspace's records;
  there is no undo. A handful of workspaces are set up by Prospektor from the
  codebase rather than through the product; those say so and cannot be deleted
  from the danger zone at all — nothing is removed and support does it for you.
- **What a deletion leaves behind: one unlinked row, and it names nobody.**
  Prospektor keeps a single bookkeeping record per workspace so it can measure
  how many customers stay and how many leave. It holds no email address, no
  company name and nothing you or your team wrote — a signup date, whether the
  workspace was paid or comped, how it was created, when a deliverable was
  first saved in it, and the dates it was paused or closed. When a workspace is
  deleted, the identifier on that row is replaced with a one-way hash, so what
  remains cannot be linked back to you. Everything else — every pitch, prep,
  share, import, note and setting — is removed.
- Billing disputes and refunds are handled by a human over email — the
  support chat can gather the details but never touches money.

files.text:
# Best practices — how teams get better pitches

The studio's output quality tracks what the workspace has taught it. In
rough order of leverage:

1. **Answer the interview questions, all of them.** "What should the studio
   find for you", a deal that already worked, and how you want to sound are
   the three highest-leverage sentences in the product — every run scores
   fit against them. Open [Workspace settings](/settings) any time to sharpen
   an answer.
2. **Edit a deliverable and save it — early and often.** Saved edits become
   brand-voice examples for every future run (tone only, never facts). Three
   edited pitches teach the studio more about how your team sounds than any
   settings screen — and every edit after those three still counts, because
   a run picks the saved edits closest to the company it is working on
   rather than the three most recent.
3. **Answer the brief's open gaps.** "What the studio could not establish"
   on the workspace page lists what research could not verify — every gap
   you fill is a fact every future pitch can use.
4. **Import your network.** Warm paths only exist when
   [Your network](/network) has something in it — a pasted list takes a
   minute and immediately upgrades every finished pitch with who could make
   the introduction.
5. **Record outcomes — the losses as much as the wins.** This is the one
   that compounds. [Outcomes](/outcomes) feeds the Suggested shelf, and
   since 23 Aug 2026 a digest of your own record also rides every pitch,
   prep and inbound evaluation: what your team actually wins on, and the
   objection that actually kills your deals. A sentence typed after a call
   that went nowhere is worth more to the next draft than any settings
   screen. It never leaves the studio: the prompt forbids repeating any of it
   outward, and the compliance check flags it if a draft does anyway.
6. **Give the pitch form its two dropdowns.** Motion and value angle come
   from your own brief's vocabulary — picking them steers the draft's whole
   argument, and leaving them empty asks the studio to guess.
7. **Use bracketed placeholders as a checklist, not an annoyance.** They
   mark exactly what the studio refused to invent — numbers, names, claims.
   Filling them before sending is what makes a pitch credible.
8. **Prep the call, don't re-read the pitch.** [Call prep](/prep) compresses
   a finished pitch into the one sheet that matters for exactly the call you
   are about to take.

files.text:
# Troubleshooting — what things mean

- **Results marked "simulated"** — the deploy has no model key configured;
  the plumbing ran but nothing was researched. On the production studio this
  should never appear; if it does, that is worth reporting.
- **Blank decision-maker names** — deliberate, not a bug. A name is filled
  only when a credible source supports it; blanks are left for your own
  enrichment rather than guessed.
- **Bracketed placeholders in a draft** — facts the studio could not verify
  and refused to invent. They are listed together on the pitch so you can
  fill them before sending.
- **A run that sits on one stage for minutes** — research reads the live
  web and is the long stage; the activity line under it ("2 searches · 9
  sources read") is the sign it is alive. A run silent for twenty minutes
  is marked stopped and can be dismissed to *Did not finish*, where
  run-again lives.
- **"Drafted from a partial brief"** on a pitch — the run started before
  the workspace's research or interview finished. The pitch is real but
  worth less; sharpening the brief and running again is the fix.
- **A paused workspace** — the subscription behind it lapsed. The lock
  screen's resubscribe button reopens the same studio with everything kept.
  Shared links pause with it and come back with it.
- **"This workspace's records are temporarily unavailable"** — a storage
  outage on our side; nothing is lost. Try again shortly.
- **Someone can't sign in** — their address is probably not on the
  workspace's allowlist; the owner adds it in
  [Workspace settings](/settings). Removal takes effect immediately, and
  so does adding.
- **A share link stopped working** — it was revoked or expired. Mint a new
  one from the pitch; [Shared links](/shares) shows every link's state.
- **A recipient says a link is "not available right now"** — the workspace
  is paused, so every link it has sent is paused too. Reactivating brings
  them all back; nothing was revoked and nothing was lost.
- **No suggestions on the home screen** — normal for a brand-new workspace
  while research lands, and the shelf refills over time; running pitches
  and recording outcomes are what feed it.
- **A portfolio row that says "waiting its turn"** — normal. Three
  companies are researched at a time so none of them is rushed; the row
  starts by itself when a slot frees. You can close the tab.
- **A portfolio row that says "could not be finished"** — the workspace
  exists and works, but its research did not land. Open it and use
  *Rescan* in [Workspace settings](/settings).
- **"Skipped … — already has a workspace"** on an upload — your agency is
  already on that company's workspace, so a second one was not created.
  Switch to it from the workspace switcher.

files.name: 11-privacy.md
files.text:
# Cookies, and what is kept on your device

## The short answer

Prospektor stores six small things on the device you are reading this on, and
every one of them is either signing you in or remembering a preference you
set about your own screen. There is **no analytics, no advertising, no
session recording and no third party** — the studio's pages make no request
to any other company at all, not even for typefaces.

That is why the notice you saw on your first visit had a **Got it** button
rather than an Accept and a Reject. There is nothing optional to accept or
reject yet, and a choice over nothing is worse than no question at all.

## Seeing the list yourself

**Cookies** in the footer of any page, or the address
`studio.prospektor.ai/#cookies`, opens the full list: what each item is
called, whether it is a cookie or browser storage, what it is for, and how
long it stays. It is the same list the code works from, so it cannot drift
out of date without a test failing.

| What | Kind | For | Kept |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pps_session` | Cookie | Keeps you signed in, and remembers which workspace you picked | 12 hours |
| `pps_oauth_state` | Cookie | Protects the Google sign-in round trip | 10 minutes |
| `pps_share` | Cookie | Remembers which shared pitch sent you to sign in, so you land back on it | 10 minutes |
| `pps-theme` | Local storage | This device's light/dark choice | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-library-sort` | Local storage | How this device likes the library sorted | Until you clear site data |
| `pps-consent` | Local storage | Your answer to the cookie notice, and when you gave it | 12 months |

The two `pps-` preferences are stored on the device, **not against your
account** — your colleagues are unaffected, and nobody, including us, can
look up how you like the studio to appear.

## Changing your mind

Click **Cookies** in the footer. Whatever you chose, the same panel that set
it will unset it, from any page, with no sign-in and no email to anyone. If
you clear your browser's site data, the answer goes with it and you will be
asked again on your next visit.

You will also be asked again if twelve months pass, or if we ever change what
we store — an answer to one version of this notice is not treated as an
answer to a different one.

## If your browser says no on your behalf

Some browsers and extensions send a **Global Privacy Control** signal, which
is a standing "do not sell or share my information". Prospektor reads that as
a refusal of everything optional and records it that way without asking you
again. You can still turn something on from the Cookies panel if you want to.

## Why there is a panel at all if nothing is optional

Because of what comes next. The panel is the gate anything measured would
have to come through, and it is switched on before there is anything to
measure rather than after. If Prospektor ever adds an analytics tool, three
things happen at once and none of them is optional for us: it appears in that
list with its name and its purpose, the notice turns into a real Accept and
Reject with equal weight, and it does not load at all until you have said yes.

## Share links

If someone sent you a Prospektor link and you are reading their work rather
than using the studio, the same is true of that page: strictly necessary
cookies only, no third-party requests, and the same **Cookies** link in its
footer. The person who shared it can see that the link was opened; what they
see, and what the sender's workspace knows about you, is set out in the
[privacy policy](https://prospektor.ai/privacy/#viewers).
